topic.resolution: Jesus rose bodily from the dead

turns.speech:
Thank you. My case is an inference to the best explanation. I'll set out four historical data points that most critical scholars accept, whether or not they believe, and then argue that the bodily resurrection explains them better than the alternatives.

**1. Very early testimony.** In 1 Corinthians 15:3–8, written around AD 53–55, Paul passes on a tradition he says he "received": Christ died, was buried, was raised on the third day, and appeared to Cephas, the Twelve, more than 500 at once, James, and then Paul himself. Scholars from Gerd Lüdemann to James D. G. Dunn date this formula to within a few years of the crucifixion. Paul also says he met Cephas and James in Jerusalem (Galatians 1:18–19). This is not a late legend. It is a claim that witnesses who could be named were making from the very start.

**2. The empty tomb.** I'll be candid that this is more contested than the appearances. Still, a majority of specialists accept it. Mark's account is early. Women are the primary witnesses, which is embarrassing given how their testimony was treated (compare Josephus, *Antiquities* 4.219). And the earliest Jewish counter-claim, that the disciples stole the body (Matthew 28:11–15; Justin, *Dialogue with Trypho* 108), already grants that the tomb was empty. Proclaiming a resurrection in Jerusalem would also have been hard to sustain if the body was still in a known grave.

**3. Appearances to individuals and to groups.** Bart Ehrman writes that it is historically certain some disciples believed they saw Jesus alive after his death. Grief hallucinations do happen, but they are generally private experiences. They don't readily explain shared group appearances, or the conversion of hostile outsiders: Paul the persecutor, and James the skeptical brother (Mark 3:21; John 7:5).

**4. The origin of the belief itself.** N. T. Wright's *The Resurrection of the Son of God* (2003) shows that in Second Temple Judaism, "resurrection" meant a bodily, end-of-days event for all the righteous. It did not mean a single man raised in the middle of history. A crucified Messiah was a falsified Messiah (Deuteronomy 21:23; Galatians 3:13). Yet these Jewish followers proclaimed a bodily raised Messiah at once. Paul's "spiritual body" (1 Cor 15:44) is a transformed body, not an immaterial one: what is "sown" is what is "raised." Some of them, including James (Josephus, *Antiquities* 20.200), died rather than give it up.

Theft, wrong tomb, swoon, and hallucination each explain one data point at most, and each strains against the others. The resurrection hypothesis explains all four.

Two concessions up front. First, historical method alone can't prove a miracle. How probable the resurrection is depends partly on your background view of whether God exists. That's why I'll argue theism is at least a live option, and that the event fits a context of real religious meaning. Second, the Gospels show real discrepancies in their details. Those affect the secondary details, not the core claims listed above.

I invite my opponent to offer one naturalistic account that explains all four facts together.

turns.speech:
Thank you. I'll start by accepting a lot of my opponent's case. Jesus was crucified. 1 Corinthians 15:3–7 preserves a tradition that is very early, plausibly from within the first few years. His followers sincerely believed they had seen him. So my disagreement is about the inference, not the data.

**1. The prior probability matters, and my opponent has granted it.** A bodily resurrection isn't a normal historical claim. It asks us to believe that the laws governing corpses were suspended once. Ancient texts that are early and sincere still record many events no historian accepts. Since history can't prove a miracle, the real question is whether ordinary human processes could produce these beliefs. They plainly can.

**2. The earliest evidence is visionary, not bodily.** Paul is our only eyewitness source. He puts his own experience in the same list, using the same verb, *ōphthē*, "he appeared." Paul's own experience was a revelation "in me" (Galatians 1:16). Acts describes it as a light and a voice that his companions did not see in the same way (Acts 9:7; 22:9). Paul never mentions an empty tomb, women, or Jesus eating. Look at the order the texts were written in. Mark (c. 70) has no appearance at all and ends with the women telling no one (16:8). Matthew adds guards and an earthquake. Luke and John add a Jesus who can be touched and who eats fish. The Gospel of Peter has a giant figure followed by a talking cross. That is how legends grow.

**3. The tomb is weak evidence.** Romans often left crucified bodies exposed, but there were exceptions. Josephus (*Jewish War* 4.317) shows that Jews buried even crucified men, so I grant that some burial is plausible. A hasty or criminal burial, though, is not a tomb anyone could later point to (see Bart Ehrman, *How Jesus Became God*, ch. 4). The "stolen body" polemic is a reply to the Christian story, decades later. It is not an independent check on the tomb.

**4. My naturalistic account, as requested.** Grief visions are very common. Studies of the bereaved find that a large minority report sensing or seeing the dead. Peter, grieving and probably guilty after his denial, has such an experience. In a small, tightly bound apocalyptic group, the report spreads and others have their own experiences. Dale Allison, a Christian scholar, documents collective bereavement experiences in *Resurrecting Jesus* (2005). Collective sightings also occur in Marian apparitions such as Zeitoun (1968), which my opponent presumably does not count as real. Paul's experience is a vision. On Wright's argument: these were apocalyptic Jews who expected the general resurrection soon. Visions of Jesus would naturally be read as its "firstfruits" (1 Cor 15:20). Mark 6:14–16 shows that an individual being "raised" was already thinkable. Leon Festinger's *When Prophecy Fails* (1956) shows that groups often strengthen their commitment after a disconfirmation.

Martyrdom shows sincerity, which I've already granted. It does not show that the belief was true. Each step in my account is a documented human behavior. The resurrection hypothesis needs a God who exists and chose to act. That assumption carries the whole explanation.

turns.speech:
I'll take your three questions first.

**1. Is there pre-Gospel evidence that the appearances were bodily?** You're right that Paul never describes them. I concede that the evidence before the Gospels is inferential, not descriptive. Here is the inference. The formula runs "died... was buried... was raised." For a Pharisee, putting "buried" before "raised" points to the thing in the grave coming out of it. In 1 Corinthians 15:42–44 the same subject is "sown" and then "raised." Romans 8:11 speaks of life given to "your mortal bodies," and Philippians 3:21 says our body will be conformed to "his glorious body." Paul also keeps the appearances apart from his ongoing "visions and revelations" (2 Cor 12:1). He calls his own appearance the "last of all" (1 Cor 15:8), and calling it last means the series had closed. A Jesus who appeared only in visions would have no reason to stop appearing.

**2. Zeitoun.** I don't know what happened at Zeitoun, and I won't call it a hoax. But it isn't a parallel. There, crowds who were primed to expect Mary saw a light at a distance and argued over what it was. In 1 Corinthians 15, a man the witnesses knew is recognized and gives a commission. He also appears to people with no expectation at all, or with hostile ones: James and Paul.

**3. Prior.** On naturalism the prior is close to zero, and I grant that openly. On theism, given Jesus's unique claims and his context, I'd put it very roughly at 1 in 100 to 1 in 1,000. Those figures are a judgment call, not a calculation. For a careful treatment of the likelihoods, see Timothy and Lydia McGrew in the *Blackwell Companion to Natural Theology* (2009).

**Rebuttal.** Grief explains Peter. It doesn't explain Paul, who wasn't grieving, or James, who didn't believe. On Festinger: groups that suffer a disconfirmation fall back on categories they already have. Mark 6:14–16 is Herod guessing that John had come back. Nobody exalted John as Lord or proclaimed the end-time resurrection had begun in him. Allison himself judges an empty tomb more likely than not. If I've misremembered how strongly he puts that, I'll correct it.

**Questions.** Why did Paul put "buried" in the formula at all if the body stayed where it was laid? And what triggered Paul's vision?

I'll answer your two questions first.

**Why "buried"?** Partly to confirm that Jesus really died. "Died and was buried" is a standard Jewish pairing for that (compare Acts 2:29 on David). But I'll grant the stronger point. A Pharisee like Paul probably did assume the body left the grave. That tells us what Paul believed. It doesn't tell us anyone checked. Once you believe God raised Jesus, believing the tomb is empty follows from that, without anyone needing to look. Paul's own model also cuts against a reanimated corpse. "You do not sow the body that is to be" (1 Cor 15:37), and "flesh and blood cannot inherit the kingdom" (15:50). The body is transformed and continuous, yes. But that is a theological claim, not a report of what anyone saw.

**What triggered Paul's vision?** I'll be honest: we can't psychoanalyze Paul, so any answer is speculation. Here is what we do know. He was a visionary by temperament. He reports heavenly ascents (2 Cor 12:1–4), speaks in tongues "more than all of you" (1 Cor 14:18), and hears the Lord speak to him (2 Cor 12:9). A zealot who was close to the people he persecuted, and possibly troubled by them, is a recognizable psychological profile. The trigger is unknown, not inexplicable.

**Rebuttal.** "Last of all" doesn't show the appearances had ended. Christians kept seeing Jesus afterwards: Stephen (Acts 7:56), Paul in a trance in the Temple (Acts 22:17–18), John (Rev 1). Paul's "last" most likely asserts his rank as an apostle (15:9). On James, Acts 1:14 already puts Jesus's brothers among the believers. We have no account of an appearance to James, and nothing shows his conversion came after one. On Allison, you remember him correctly. He leans cautiously toward the empty tomb, and I accept that.

**Questions.** (1) Given Acts 7 and 22, what makes Paul's Damascus experience different in kind from later visions of Jesus? (2) What evidence shows that James's belief began after an appearance, not before?

turns.speech:
I'll answer your two questions first.

**1. Damascus versus later visions.** I'll be honest about how far this goes. Nothing in the *experience* itself has to set Damascus apart. Acts describes light and a voice, not touch. The difference lies in how Paul and Luke classify it. Paul treats "Have I not seen Jesus our Lord?" (1 Cor 9:1) as a credential that makes him an apostle. He never makes that claim for his later revelations (2 Cor 12:1). Luke keeps the categories apart too. The appearances end with the ascension (Acts 1:3, 9). Acts 22:17 is explicitly "in a trance" (*ekstasis*). Stephen sees Jesus in heaven, not on earth. You may be right that "last of all" partly asserts Paul's rank. Still, paired with *ektrōma*, "untimely born" (15:8), it most naturally marks him as late and out of sequence. So the distinction is one the early community drew, not one I can read off the phenomenology.

**2. James.** No account of the appearance survives. The one in the Gospel of the Hebrews, quoted by Jerome (*De viris illustribus* 2), is late and legendary. Here is the evidence I do have. The Gospels show James unbelieving during the ministry (Mark 3:21, 31–35; John 7:5). 1 Corinthians 15:7 lists an appearance to him. By Galatians 1:19 and 2:9 he is a "pillar." Acts 1:14 doesn't help you, because it is set *after* the appearances (1:3). I concede that "conversion through an appearance" is a probable inference, not something the texts show. That weakens James as a hostile witness.

**Pressing.** "Flesh and blood" (15:50) is a Semitic idiom for mortal human nature (compare Gal 1:16; Matt 16:17). Paul goes straight on: "*this* perishable must put on imperishability" (15:53). Your case needs a tomb nobody could check. Yet Mark names Joseph of Arimathea, a member of the Sanhedrin, as the man who buried Jesus (15:43). That is an odd thing to invent. Raymond Brown (*The Death of the Messiah*, 1994) judged the Joseph burial probably historical.

**Questions.** (1) If Joseph's burial is historical, how does your account survive a known tomb? (2) Why would visionaries in Jerusalem stress "the third day" rather than an exaltation to heaven?

I'll answer your two questions first.

**1. If Joseph's burial is historical.** That would be a real difficulty for my account, and I won't wave it away. Brown did judge the Joseph burial probably historical. But a historical Joseph doesn't give us a tomb that anyone checked. Mark 14:64 says "all" the council condemned Jesus. Acts 13:29 keeps a different tradition, in which "they," meaning the Jerusalem rulers, took him down and laid him in a tomb. That reads like a burial carried out to obey Deuteronomy 21:23, not an act of devotion. The Mishnah (Sanhedrin 6:5) describes separate burial places kept for executed criminals, though it is late and may be idealized. Also, the disciples seem to have gone back to Galilee (Mark 14:28; 16:7). Acts puts the first public preaching seven weeks later. A known tomb raises the cost of my hypothesis. A known tomb that someone checked, early, is what your argument needs, and we don't have evidence of that.

**2. Why "the third day"?** Your question assumes no one believed the body had left the grave, but I've already granted that Paul believed it. My claim is that the belief came from the visions plus theology, not from anyone inspecting the tomb. "The third day" is tied to "according to the Scriptures" (1 Cor 15:4). Hosea 6:2 says "on the third day he will raise us up," and Jonah 1:17 gives three days in the fish. It may also just record when the first vision happened. I hold that one loosely.

**Pressing.** You've now conceded that the appearances before the Gospels aren't described as physical, that Damascus doesn't differ in kind from later visions, and that James is not clearly a hostile witness. What remains is belief that an empty tomb *followed from* the resurrection, and that is exactly what my account predicts.

**Questions.** (1) Which tradition came first: Mark's sympathetic Joseph, or the hostile burial by the rulers in Acts 13:29? (2) What pre-Markan evidence shows that anyone actually visited the tomb?

I'll answer your two questions first.

**1. Which burial tradition came first?** Mark, as a written text: around 70, against Acts around 80–90. But I don't think the two conflict. The same author who wrote Acts 13:29 also has Joseph bury Jesus (Luke 23:50–53), so Luke saw no contradiction between them. A speech that sums up what "the rulers" did can include one of their members acting. Brown himself suggested that Joseph may have acted as a law-observant council member following Deuteronomy 21:23, not as a disciple. If so, your tradition and mine come together: a burial by the authorities, carried out by a named man, with the women watching where (Mark 15:47). A known grave is still the result.

**2. Pre-Markan evidence of a visit?** I concede it: no pre-Markan text reports anyone visiting the tomb. Some scholars (Rudolf Pesch, and more cautiously Brown) argue that Mark used a pre-Markan passion narrative that included the tomb, but that is disputed. My case here is inferential.

**Pressing.** You say belief in the empty tomb simply follows from belief in the resurrection. That assumes visions would be read as "raised" in the first place. Jews had other categories ready to hand. When Peter shows up at the door, the household says, "It is his angel" (Acts 12:15). Luke 24:37 has the disciples think they are seeing a "spirit." Wisdom 3:1–4 has the righteous dead at peace with God. Visions of a vindicated martyr fit "exalted," "his angel," or "his spirit" naturally. "Raised" fits only if they believed something had happened to the body. Also, the movement's leadership was in Jerusalem within weeks or months: Paul visits Cephas and James there around AD 35 (Gal 1:18–19). That is the same city where a council member's grave could be found. I grant this is partly an argument from silence.

**Questions.** (1) Why did the visions produce "raised" and not the category already available, "his angel" or "his spirit"? (2) Do you grant that the leaders were based in Jerusalem by about 35, within reach of the grave?

I'll answer your two questions first.

**1. Why "raised" and not "his angel" or "his spirit"?** This is your best point, and I grant that "raised" is a meaningful choice. It shows they believed something had happened to Jesus himself, body included. But the category was already available to them. In Daniel 12:2–3 the raised righteous "shine like the brightness of the firmament... like the stars." In 2 Maccabees 7 (vv. 9, 11, 14), *resurrection* is what martyrs are promised as their vindication. Jesus himself taught resurrection (Mark 12:18–27) and announced that the end was imminent. So: a martyred righteous man appears in luminous glory to apocalyptic followers. Martyr theology and Daniel together supply the reading "God has raised him: the end has begun." Paul's light from heaven fits Daniel's astral picture better than it fits a reanimated corpse. And Luke 24:37–43 cuts against you. Luke works hard to refute the "spirit" reading, which suggests that reading was live because the experiences were ambiguous.

**2. Jerusalem by about 35?** Yes, I grant it (Gal 1:18–19). But think about what that requires. By 35 the grave was years old. Even at Pentecost, seven weeks on, a body in a criminal burial would be badly decomposed in that climate, and I'm not sure anyone could have identified it. Believers had no reason to look, because their conviction came from the visions. The authorities had little reason to bother until the movement mattered. Acts 2:29–31 does contrast David's tomb with Jesus, but that is Luke's composition, decades later.

**Pressing.** Your case now rests on a tomb that, you concede, no early text says anyone checked. Against that you have a near-zero prior on naturalism and a theistic prior you call a judgment call. Silence can't carry that much weight.

**Questions.** (1) Doesn't Daniel 12:3 plus 2 Maccabees 7 give apocalyptic Jews a ready path from a vision of a martyr in glory to "raised"? (2) Seven weeks after burial, could anyone have identified the body?

turns.speech:
I'll answer your two questions first.

**1. Do Daniel 12 and 2 Maccabees 7 give a path from vision to "raised"?** Partly, yes. I concede the category was available. Combined with imminent expectation, a reading like "God has raised him" is not psychologically impossible. But look at what those texts mean by the word. In Daniel 12:2, those raised are the ones who "sleep in the dust of the earth." In 2 Maccabees 7:11, the third brother puts out his hands and says he hopes to get them back from God. The luminous glory in Daniel 12:3 comes *after* the bodily rising and does not replace it. So your own sources make "raised" mean the body comes out of the grave. That helps my case, because it makes the claim publicly falsifiable. What these texts lack is a single person raised ahead of everyone else, in the middle of history. That change still needs an explanation.

judges_v1.verdict:
This was an unusually honest and high-level exchange. Both debaters answered every question directly, cited sources accurately, and made real concessions. The result turns on burden of proof and on the specific wording of the resolution: a bodily resurrection.

The theist's strongest move was the origin-of-belief argument in Round 4. Jews had softer categories available ("his angel," "his spirit," exaltation), so choosing "raised" implies a claim about the body. Combined with Daniel 12:2 and 2 Maccabees 7:11, this made the claim publicly falsifiable. The theist also pressed hard on Paul as a hostile outsider whom the contagion model cannot reach, and the atheist openly admitted that gap.

The atheist kept the debate focused on the gap between what the early believers held and what happened. "A claim that could be checked is not a claim that was checked" pinpointed the weak link. By Round 8 the theist had conceded several key points. No pre-Gospel source describes a bodily encounter. No pre-Markan text reports anyone visiting the tomb. Paul's appearance, taken alone, cannot separate bodily resurrection from visionary exaltation. The atheist then argued well that Paul at most supports some post-mortem vindication, not the bodily claim the resolution makes.

The decisive point was the theist's own closing. He admitted his conclusion is conditional on theism, which he promised in Round 1 to show was "at least a live option" but then said he could not argue. Since the affirmative carries the burden, an admitted but undefended premise leaves the resolution unestablished. The atheist's account has real holes: Paul, and no documented parallel for group commissioning appearances. That keeps the margin narrow, but the atheist wins on the argument actually presented.

fallacies.name: Straw man / divide and conquer
fallacies.quote: Theft, wrong tomb, swoon, and hallucination each explain one data point at most, and each strains against the others.
fallacies.explanation: This tests naturalistic hypotheses one at a time, when the live alternative is a combined account. The atheist offered exactly that, and the theist later conceded in Round 7 that theft and swoon are non-starters, so the real comparison was with a composite.

fallacies.name: Weak analogy
fallacies.quote: Collective sightings also occur in Marian apparitions such as Zeitoun (1968), which my opponent presumably does not count as real.
fallacies.explanation: Zeitoun involved primed crowds seeing a distant light, not a group recognizing a known individual. The theist showed the disanalogy, and the atheist later conceded in Round 5 that he had no well-documented parallel.

fallacies.name: Weak analogy
fallacies.quote: When Sabbatai Zevi converted to Islam (1666) and later died, many followers reinterpreted both events rather than give up their belief
fallacies.explanation: The Sabbateans reinterpreted using unfalsifiable categories (occultation, descent into impurity) and never claimed a bodily raising or group appearances. That is the very feature at issue, as the theist pointed out.

fallacies.name: False dilemma
fallacies.quote: That invites people to check, and someone inventing a story wouldn't write that.
fallacies.explanation: This treats deliberate invention as the only alternative to accurate testimony, leaving out sincere transmission of an unverified tradition. The atheist made that point in reply.

factual_errors.claim: Some of them, including James (Josephus, Antiquities 20.200), died rather than give it up.
factual_errors.correction: Josephus, Antiquities 20.200, says James was stoned on a charge of breaking the law, brought by the high priest Ananus. It does not say he was killed for refusing to recant belief in the resurrection, or that he was offered the chance to recant. The 'died rather than give it up' framing goes beyond what the source says.

factual_errors.claim: Mark (c. 70) has no appearance at all and ends with the women telling no one (16:8).
factual_errors.correction: It is accurate that Mark has no appearance narrative. However, Mark 16:7 (and 14:28) explicitly predicts an appearance in Galilee, so it is misleading to present Mark as evidence that appearance traditions were absent at that stage. The atheist cited 16:7 himself in Round 3.

key_concessions.point: The conclusion is conditional on theism, which was not argued in this debate, so it does not persuade someone who starts from a naturalistic prior.
No pre-Markan text reports anyone visiting the tomb; the case for an early checked tomb is inferential.
Paul's appearance, taken alone, is not evidence for a bodily resurrection as opposed to visionary exaltation.
James's conversion through an appearance is an inference, not something the texts show, which weakens him as a hostile witness.
The contagion model does not reach Paul; he is the hardest datum for the account, and no trigger can be named.
There is no well-documented case of a group seeing a personally known deceased individual who gives them a commission.
The choice of 'raised' shows the early believers held that something happened to Jesus's body; this is the theist's strongest point.
Because 'raised' implied the body leaving the grave, the claim was in principle publicly falsifiable.

The atheist then argued that Paul at most supports theism plus some post-mortem vindication, not a bodily rising. Together with the earlier concession that no pre-Markan text reports a checked tomb, this left the bodily element, which is the resolution's actual claim, resting on inference alone, with the theism premise conceded as unargued.

best_argument.theist: The origin-of-belief argument. Second Temple Jews had softer, unfalsifiable categories for a vindicated martyr ('his angel,' 'his spirit,' exaltation; Acts 12:15, Luke 24:37, Wisdom 3), and failed movements like the Sabbateans reached for such categories. The disciples instead proclaimed that one man had been 'raised' in the middle of history. On their own sources (Dan 12:2, 2 Macc 7:11), that meant the body leaving the grave, and they proclaimed it in Jerusalem, where the burial took place. Combined with Paul, a hostile outsider beyond the reach of group contagion, this places a real explanatory cost on the naturalistic account.

Every pre-Gospel datum ('buried,' 'raised,' the 500) establishes what believers held, not that anyone checked a tomb or met a physical body. The only firsthand appearance (Paul's) was a post-ascension vision that cannot distinguish bodily resurrection from exaltation. Touch and eating appear only 40 to 60 years later, in accounts that disagree. Since the resolution claims a bodily rising and its probability depends on a theism the affirmative did not defend, the burden is not met.
